Though it is rather inconvenient to access the beach from wherever you might stay. If you are willing to trade a little more emf exposure for convenient beach access go with San Blas. If I remember correctly any place away from San Salvador and the airport are sufficient for getting better (watch out for cell towers of course) but the beach is ideal because you don't have to chase the sun and the volcanic sand has good magnetism. Healthy Food​There are regenerative / organic food options in El Salvador but expect to pay a hefty premium. There is a small chain of health food stores called Soya that I would recommend. The one by San Blas hosts a farmer's market regularly. Also, check out the Bitcoin Farmer's Market. Language Barrier​Once you leave the airport, there aren't many people who speak English. You will want to learn how to use Google Translate or a similar app to communicate. The locals don't seem to mind. Also, expect to have prices raised on you for being a foreigner. Transportation​Renting a car was absolutely NOT worth it. If you have never driven in a 3rd world country just use Uber. They are dirt cheap in ES and way less of a headache. So you have an idea: it cost me $27 to go an hour from the airport to San Blas. You could use the buses but I would recommend against it. If the drivers are in a hurry, they will start driving before you fully get off the bus which can be dangerous. Emergency Medical​You definitely want to know where the nearest emergency room while your there. I wasn't able to find any on the coast. The public emergency rooms are of questionable quality so I would suggest the private ones. Expect to pay up front and in cash. And remember that not all of them welcome foreigners. I used these two lists to locate a good emergency room for me: List 1, List 2. Internet Connectivity​If you buy an international package for your current carrier it usually runs relatively expensive ($40/wk). I used Jetpac and got the $30 plan for one month of coverage. Easy peasy set up if you have a recent phone that supports eSIM. That's all!

posts.text: Hi everyone — my name is Sydney Spratt, I’m 25 years old, and I’m really grateful to be here. I was born and raised in Orlando, Florida. I had a beautiful childhood,, outside constantly, thanks to my dad who owns a personal training business and my aunt who took my cousin and me on endless adventures, summers at the beach, visiting family in north Carolina and Missouri . My mom was an esthetician, so I grew up with sunscreen, hats, and sunglasses being mandatory. At the time, none of us thought twice about it. My mental health struggles began around 2016. Over time, I noticed they always showed up in the winter. Even in Florida, the seasonal change hit me hard. Looking back, that pattern makes much more sense than the psychiatric labels ever did. In high school, I spent more time indoors, and during marching band (I was on the drumline) we were drenched in sunscreen like an assembly line. That’s when my depression and anxiety really began. I went to Florida State University, and college intensified everything,, uncertainty about my future, drinking and smoking weed for the first time, and a huge amount of screen time. After a short questionnaire, a campus therapist immediately suggested Zoloft. The speed of that diagnosis stayed with me. Florence, Art, and Tattoos​ In 2019, I lived in Florence for five months. It was one of the most transformative times of my life. I’ve always been enthralled by art history, and being surrounded by that culture felt like a homecoming. While there, I got two tattoos — part of what has become eight thoughtful, meaningful tattoos (not sleeves, just pieces I love). The COVID Years​ When COVID hit, school moved online and I worked at a grocery store full of natural light. I always dimmed the overhead lights — I’ve hated artificial lighting since childhood and used to wear yellow-tinted glasses in school, much to the annoyance of my teachers. That year, I was extremely productive. I got straight A’s, had a consistent sleep schedule, ran a cycling club, and balanced work and school. Structure grounded me. I didn’t understand yet how much my environment influenced me, but I see it clearly now. Psychiatric Labels & Mismatched Explanations​ Eventually I crashed. A psychiatrist diagnosed me with bipolar disorder. At the time, it felt like the end of my life. Now I see it differently — I’ve reframed that label completely. I don’t view it as a disease; I view it as a sign that I’m profoundly sensitive to my environment, to light, to EMFs, and to seasonal shifts. Throughout college, my medications constantly changed. One antipsychotic that dissolved on my tongue made me feel like Godzilla — chemically overloaded and enraged. My psychiatrist once said, “You’re extremely hard to read,” which made me laugh, because I never trusted him enough to tell him how I truly felt. He was always listening for symptoms, not for truth. Eventually, the anxiety got so severe that I asked my mom to take me to the hospital. I stayed for four days. Compared to others, I was stable — I slept, ate, participated. It wasn’t traumatic, which I know is rare. Afterward, I attended an IOP program with other college students, which genuinely helped me. That community understood what I was experiencing. And somehow, after years of ups and downs, I finally finished my degree in commercial entrepreneurship in 2023. Amazon & The Breaking Point​ After graduation I started working for Amazon — the kind of job I thought I “should” have, the kind my family would be proud of. I traveled: Seattle, Tampa, Orlando, Tallahassee. I was surrounded by warehouse lighting, screens, radios clipped to my head, and nonstop artificial environments. That period culminated in what psychiatry would label my most intense manic episode — but for me, it felt like an awakening paired with a spiritual rupture. When I was searching the term misophonia, I came across a related term — misokinesia — which refers to an intense discomfort triggered by visual movement, like fidgeting, repetitive gestures, or body language. Reading about it instantly brought back a vivid memory from high school — this was over 30 years ago, long before AirPods or constant tech were part of my life. I always struggled to focus in classrooms where there was a sign language interpreter. While they were essential for deaf students, my brain locked onto the motion and couldn’t disengage. I would completely miss what the teacher was saying. It wasn’t intentional — it was like the movement had urgency and my brain prioritized it over everything else. At the time, I was told I just needed to “suck it up.” Teachers and even my mother made me feel ashamed, like I was being insensitive or selfish. But looking back, I realize: it wasn’t about the interpreter—it was about how my brain filtered (or didn’t filter) sensory input. I wasn’t being mean; I had an undiagnosed sensory gating issue. I now see that I may have been the one with the disability — not in morality or attitude, but in neurobiology. So my question to the group (and to Jack, if he sees this): Is misokinesia connected to misophonia through the same root cause — degraded melanin, circadian mismatch, or mitochondrial disorganization? Or is this just a tangent I shouldn’t chase? I don’t want to get lost down a rabbit hole of labels, but the resonance with my past is strong. And I wonder if others have experienced similar visual triggers alongside auditory ones. Thanks again for helping me see this part of myself more clearly.
